title: Sustainability

definition.text: Sustainability is the ability to keep going over a long time; today it usually means a state in which environment, economy and society all continue to exist long into the future.

facts.text: The word comes from the Latin sustinere; 'to sustain' can mean to maintain, support, uphold or endure.
It is a normative concept: it rests on what people value and want for the future.
Many definitions stress the environmental side, including tackling climate change and biodiversity loss.
The economic side is controversial, and scholars debate it as weak versus strong sustainability.
Sustainability is hard to measure because it is complex, contextual and dynamic, and there is no fixed set of indicators.
Critics call the idea vague, a mere buzzword, or an impossible goal.
UNESCO frames sustainability as the long-term goal and sustainable development as the pathways to reach it.

contested_note: Critics argue the concept is too vague to guide action and may be an impossible goal.

title: Sustainable development

definition.text: Sustainable development is an approach to growth and human development that aims to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

facts.text: The widely used definition comes from the 1987 Brundtland Report, Our Common Future, which stresses the essential needs of the world's poor and the limits technology and social organisation place on the environment.
It tries to balance economic development, environmental protection and social well-being.
Its roots lie in 17th- and 18th-century European ideas of sustainable forest management, such as von Carlowitz's sustained-yield forestry.
The 1992 Earth Summit in Rio began the Rio Process that put sustainable development on the international agenda.
It is the foundational concept of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals adopted by all UN members in 2015.
Critics ask what exactly is to be sustained, and argue that no use of a non-renewable resource can be sustainable since any extraction eventually exhausts a finite stock.
The debate assumes societies manage economic, social and natural capital, which may not substitute for one another and whose use may be irreversible.

contested_note: Scholars understand the concept in many ways and criticise it from several angles, including what is to be sustained.

definition.text: The three dimensions of sustainability are the environmental, social and economic areas that scholars usually distinguish within the concept.

facts.text: Writers also call them pillars, components, aspects or goals; all mean the same here.
The familiar three-circle Venn diagram first appeared in a 1987 article by the economist Edward Barbier.
The paradigm has few theoretical foundations, though it dominates the literature.
Agenda 21 (1992) and Agenda 2030 (2015) both frame sustainability through economic, social and environmental dimensions.

definition.text: The nested model ranks the three dimensions of sustainability, drawing the economy inside society and society inside the environment.

facts.text: Many publications treat the environmental dimension, ecological or planetary integrity, as the most important, so it sets limits on economic and social development.
The SDG 'wedding cake' model likewise shows the economy as a subset of society, and society as a subset of the biosphere.
A 2022 assessment argued the SDGs fail to make protecting planetary integrity an end in itself.

title: Economic dimension of sustainability

definition.text: The economic dimension of sustainability concerns how economic development fits with protecting the environment and meeting basic needs, and it is controversial.

facts.text: The controversy arises because 'development' can be read as just economic growth, which can promote a system bad for the environment.
Economic development can reduce hunger and energy poverty, which is why SDG 8 calls for growth, measured partly by real GDP per capita.
The challenge is to expand economic activity while cutting its environmental impact.
The Brundtland Report holds that poverty both causes and results from environmental problems.

contested_note: Sources disagree whether economic growth belongs in sustainability or undermines it.

definition.text: Sustainability barriers are the reasons sustainability is so hard to achieve.

facts.text: Intrinsic barriers come from nature's complexity and the human condition, such as the value-action gap, where people do not act on their convictions.
Extrinsic barriers can be overcome, for example by putting a price on the consumption of public goods.
Competitive market economies carry a structural imperative to grow, which inhibits needed change.
Political pressure favours the short term over the long term.

definition.text: A sustainability transition (or transformation) is a deep, system-wide change in technology, economy, society, values and goals towards sustainability.

facts.text: It must happen at every scale, from local communities to global governance institutions.
It is politically debated, since stakeholders may disagree on goals and methods and it can challenge existing power and resource distribution.
It may only work if far-reaching lifestyle changes accompany technological advances.

definition.text: Daly's operational principles are three rules for sustainable development published by Herman Daly in 1990.

facts.text: Renewable resources should be harvested no faster than they regenerate, giving a sustainable yield.
Use of non-renewable resources should be matched by equivalent development of renewable substitutes.
Waste generation should not exceed the environment's assimilative capacity.
An unsustainable situation arises when natural capital is used up faster than it can be replenished.
